records.place: Sauternes, on the left bank of the Garonne, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château d'Yquem
wine.classification: Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification, a rank held by no other estate
wine.grapes: Sémillon, about three quarters, with Sauvignon Blanc for the rest.
wine.sites: One hill above the village of Sauternes, its soils varying from plot to plot, sandy in some and clay in others, near where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and autumn mists bring the noble rot.
wine.making: Pickers pass through the vines in successive rounds over several weeks, taking only berries shrivelled by noble rot. Each day's pick is pressed and fermented in new oak barrels; the barrels kept for Yquem then age for about twenty months in the estate's cellar before the blend is bottled at the château. In a year judged too poor, nothing is released under the name.
wine.glass: Apricot, saffron, barley sugar and orange marmalade over pineapple, vanilla and crème brûlée; luscious and deep, yet carried by fresh acidity to a long finish of honey and bitter orange peel.
wine.ageing: Delicious from release, it deepens to amber over decades and can last a century in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, an old bottle a degree or two warmer; no need to decant a young bottle; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of five communes on the Ciron; by law its wine is sweet.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Ranked alone above every other Sauternes and Barsac in 1855, Château d'Yquem is mostly Sémillon, picked berry by berry over many passes as noble rot takes hold. It tastes of apricot, saffron and marmalade, and can last a century.
records.story: In 1593 a member of the Sauvage family, local nobles, was given the feudal tenure of Yquem, as the estate tells it, and in 1711 the family became its full owners. In 1785 the Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family; widowed three years later, she ran the estate herself. In December 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), the American minister in Paris, ordered Yquem for himself, and in 1790 he ordered thirty dozen bottles more from the estate for President George Washington (1732 to 1799). In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers set Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, a rank made for it and never shared. The family kept its discipline: many passes through the vines at each harvest, and no wine at all under the name in years judged too poor, nine of them in the twentieth century, from 1910 to 1992. In 1959 it added a dry white, Y, sold as Bordeaux. In 1996 relatives sold a majority to the luxury group LVMH, which took control in 1999 after a court battle with the head of the family, and in 2012 Yquem again declined a vintage. For a sommelier it shows plainly what Sauternes asks: noble rot, patience and the nerve to sell nothing in a poor year.

others.name: Y du Château d'Yquem
others.note: The dry white of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, first made in 1959 and sold as Bordeaux, never as Sauternes; a different wine, not a second wine.

traps: Premier Cru Supérieur is Yquem's alone; the eleven estates below it are Premiers Crus.
Y is a dry wine sold as Bordeaux, not Sauternes, and it is not a second wine of Yquem.
Yquem releases nothing under its name in a year it judges too poor, so a missing vintage is a decision, not a lost bottle.

cards.front: Château d'Yquem: what rank did the 1855 classification give it?

questions.q: A guest asks how Château d'Yquem gathers grapes for its sweet wine. Which answer fits?
opts: Many passes through the vines for nobly rotten berries
One early pick of sound, ripe bunches
Frozen grapes picked on a winter night
Grapes dried on straw mats after harvest

questions.exp: The Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family in 1785, and they held Yquem until relatives sold a majority to LVMH in 1996; the Sauvages held it before them.

wine.name: Château Climens
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon alone, with no Sauvignon Blanc at all.
wine.sites: One block on the Barsac plateau: red, iron rich clay and sand over a shelf of fissured limestone.
wine.making: Picked in several passes for nobly rotten berries, each pass and each parcel is fermented apart in oak barrels, about a third of them new. The lots are raised in barrel for twenty months to two years and kept apart until a late blend, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Lemon curd, quince and candied ginger over acacia honey, white peach and a little saffron; sweet but airy, with bright acidity running through it and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fresh in youth, it gains honey and dried apricot over twenty years and keeps for decades after.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The commune's own appellation; a Barsac estate may print Barsac or Sauternes, and Climens prints Barsac.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant.

records.table: Made from Sémillon alone on red sand and clay over limestone, Château Climens is the Barsac Premier Cru its admirers call the Lord of Barsac. Sweet yet light on its feet, it tastes of lemon curd, quince and candied ginger.
records.story: Climens lies on the Barsac plateau, where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and the autumn mists that follow bring noble rot to the grapes. Barsac's soils are thin over limestone, and its wines are known for tension rather than weight. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Climens among the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, beneath Yquem alone. The Gounouilhou family of Bordeaux held it for decades after, until 1971, when it was bought by another Bordeaux family that already held growths of the Médoc. From 1992 a daughter of that family ran it. She kept the vineyard to Sémillon alone, picked in many passes, and kept each pass and each parcel apart in barrel until a late blend, and in the 2010s she turned the farming to biodynamics. In 2022 the family sold a majority of the estate to new owners. Through each change of hands Climens has held to one idea: that Barsac's limestone and Sémillon alone can make a sweet wine that feels weightless. A candidate should take one rule from it: Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac, never required.

others.name: Cyprès de Climens
others.note: The second wine, Sémillon alone from the same vineyard.

traps: A Barsac estate may label its wine Barsac or Sauternes; an estate elsewhere in Sauternes may not use Barsac.
Climens is Sémillon alone: do not describe it as a Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc blend.

cards.front: Château Climens: what grape, and on what soil?
cards.back: Sémillon alone, on red, iron rich clay and sand over the fissured limestone of the Barsac plateau.

cards.front: What two names may a Barsac estate such as Climens print on its label?
cards.back: Barsac or Sauternes; an estate in the other four communes may use only Sauternes.

questions.q: A guest asks how much Sauvignon Blanc goes into Château Climens. What do you answer?
opts: About a quarter, as at Yquem

Most of it, with a little Muscadelle
questions.exp: Climens is planted to Sémillon alone, which shows that Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac but never required; a quarter is close to Yquem's share.

questions.q: In 1971 Château Climens was bought by owners who held it for half a century. Who were they?
questions.exp: The Lurton family, owners of several Médoc growths, bought Climens in 1971 and sold a majority in 2022; AXA bought Suduiraut in 1992, and LVMH took Yquem in the 1990s.

wine.name: Château Coutet
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon, the great majority, with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle.
wine.sites: One block around the château and its medieval tower on the Barsac plateau, over the limestone that runs close beneath the commune.
wine.making: Picked in several passes for nobly rotten berries, it is raised for about eighteen months in oak barrels, a share of them new, before bottling at the château. In rare years the most concentrated Sémillon of the two oldest parcels is picked on a day of its own and bottled apart as Cuvée Madame.
wine.glass: Lime, grapefruit and acacia over apricot, honeysuckle and a little beeswax; sweet but taut, with lively acidity and a long, clean finish of candied lemon.
wine.ageing: Bright and appealing in its first five years, it gains honey and marmalade with age and keeps for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; serve it straight from the bottle, with no decanting; a small tulip glass.

label.means: The commune appellation Coutet uses; Barsac wine may also be sold as Sauternes.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant.

records.table: Around a medieval tower on the Barsac plateau grows Château Coutet, mostly Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle. Sweet but taut, lime and apricot over limestone, it bottles a richer selection, Cuvée Madame, only in rare years.
records.story: Coutet began as a fortress while Aquitaine belonged to the English crown, in the thirteenth century by the estate's account, and its square, battlemented tower still stands in the courtyard. Confiscated by the state in 1794, it later passed by inheritance to a Lur-Saluces, of the family that held Yquem. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Coutet a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac, beside Climens, the two Barsac estates of that rank. The Lur-Saluces kept it until the early 1920s, when it passed to the family of a Lyon industrialist, and a lady of that family owned it until 1977. In her honour, as the estate tells it, the vineyard workers gave her a day's work at harvest, picking the most concentrated grapes of the two oldest Sémillon parcels, and from 1943 that pick became Cuvée Madame, made only in rare years. In 1977 the Baly family bought Coutet and kept the tradition. Coutet speaks for Barsac's own appellation: sweet wine with the tension of limestone, less broad than the Sauternes of the hills, and the right of a Barsac estate to print Sauternes instead if it wishes.

others.name: Cuvée Madame
others.note: A rare selection of the most concentrated Sémillon of the two oldest parcels, first made in 1943 and only in rare years since.

others.name: La Chartreuse de Coutet
others.note: The second wine, sweet like the grand vin.

others.name: Opalie de Château Coutet
others.note: A dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux.

traps: Barsac is one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes appellation, and it also has its own.
Cuvée Madame is not made every year, and it is a separate selection, not the estate's standard wine.

cards.front: Château Coutet: what is Cuvée Madame, and whom does it honour?
cards.back: The most concentrated Sémillon of its two oldest parcels, first made in 1943 and only in rare years, named for the lady of the house who owned Coutet until 1977.

wine.name: Château Suduiraut
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon, the great majority, with Sauvignon for the rest; the estate grows Sauvignon Blanc and a little Sauvignon Gris.
wine.sites: A broad estate in Preignac whose vines run to the edge of Yquem's, on gravelly, sandy clay where the Ciron's mists bring noble rot in most autumns.
wine.making: Picked in many passes for nobly rotten berries, the must is fermented for two to three weeks in French oak barrels, half of them new. The wine is then raised for sixteen to twenty months in barrels half new and half used once, as the estate's sheets give it, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, roasted pineapple and honey over saffron, vanilla and orange peel; rich and broad, with an oily texture held up by acidity and a long, sweet finish of marmalade.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy young, it turns to amber, marmalade and toffee over twenty to thirty years and lasts far longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; decanting is not needed; a white wine glass, filled no more than a third.

label.means: The appellation of five communes on the Ciron, Preignac among them; its wine is sweet by law.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant.

records.table: Pour Château Suduiraut for the rich side of Sauternes: Sémillon led, from Preignac vines that run to the edge of Yquem's. Expect candied apricot, roasted pineapple and honey on an oily texture, beside foie gras or a blue cheese.
records.story: In 1580 a marriage brought this Preignac estate to the Suduiraut family, whose name it carries. During the Fronde, the civil wars of 1648 to 1653, the old manor was plundered and burnt, and in 1670 a grandson of that marriage built a new château, framed by formal gardens in the French manner attributed to André Le Nôtre (1613 to 1700), the gardener of Versailles, or to his workshop. In the eighteenth century it passed to a nephew, and for a time, by the estate's account, its wine was sold as Cru du Roy. The vineyard runs to the border of Yquem, and the Ciron's mists that settle there bring noble rot in most autumns. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Suduiraut a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac. It stayed in private hands until 1992, when it was bought by AXA Millésimes, the wine estates of the French insurance group, whose first purchase had been Pichon Baron in Pauillac in 1987. The new owners kept the house style, broad Sémillon picked late in many passes, and from 2004 made a dry white of the old vines, S de Suduiraut, sold as Bordeaux. Set beside Climens or Coutet, Suduiraut gives the other face of the district: Preignac's breadth against the tension of Barsac across the Ciron.

others.name: Castelnau de Suduiraut
others.note: The second wine, Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from the same estate.

others.name: S de Suduiraut
others.note: A dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from the estate's old vines, made since 2004 by its own account and sold as Bordeaux.

traps: The five Sauternes communes are Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac; Suduiraut is in Preignac.
Suduiraut is a Premier Cru, not a Premier Cru Supérieur: that rank is Yquem's alone.
S de Suduiraut is dry and sold as Bordeaux; it is not the estate's sweet wine.

wine.name: Château Gilette Crème de Tête
wine.grapes: Mainly Sémillon, with a little Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.
wine.sites: A small vineyard in the commune of Preignac, picked in passes for nobly rotten berries like the classed growths around it.
wine.making: Fermented without oak, the wine is moved into concrete vats and kept there for about fifteen to twenty years, sometimes longer, before it is bottled, so that it reaches the market already mature.
wine.glass: Crème brûlée, dried apricot and orange marmalade over toffee, quince paste and a little coffee; deep, mellow and long, with a freshness that belies its years in vat.
wine.ageing: Released already mature, decades after the harvest, it is ready to drink and holds for many years more in bottle.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, an old bottle a degree or two warmer; decant gently only if a crust has formed; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The name the estate gives its leading selection of sweet wine.
The appellation; Gilette was not ranked in 1855 and prints no classification.

records.table: Kept for many years in concrete vats and never in oak, Château Gilette's Crème de Tête reaches the list already mature. The small Preignac estate stood outside the 1855 list, and its wine tastes of crème brûlée and dried apricot, fresh even after decades.
records.story: When the Bordeaux brokers ranked the sweet wines in 1855, Gilette, in Preignac, one of the five communes of Sauternes, was not among the estates listed, and since that list has never been reopened it has stayed outside it. The decree of 30 September 1936 that first recognised the Sauternes appellation gave it the same name as Yquem, and what has made Gilette known is not rank but time. For generations the estate has been in the hands of the Médeville family, growers of Preignac. In the 1930s, as the family tells it, the Depression left Bordeaux in a slump, and the family built concrete vats in place of oak barrels. The wine aged there more slowly than in wood, and the family has kept its sweet wine in concrete ever since, often for fifteen to twenty years before bottling, so that a Gilette reaches a list already decades old. Its leading selection is bottled as Crème de Tête. The result is a Sauternes aged without oak: deep and mellow, yet with a freshness that surprises a guest who reads the vintage. It gives a list the rare chance to offer mature Sauternes without a cellar of its own.

Crème de Tête is aged in concrete vats, not in oak barrels.

cards.front: Château Gilette Crème de Tête: in what vessels is it aged, and for how long?
cards.back: Concrete vats, never oak, for about fifteen to twenty years before it is bottled and released.

cards.front: Was Château Gilette ranked in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac?
cards.back: No: it stood outside the list in 1855 and has stayed outside it, since the list has never been reopened.

questions.exp: Gilette ages its Crème de Tête for fifteen to twenty years in concrete vats and releases it mature; it is a single vintage, not a solera.

questions.q: Château Gilette was left unranked in 1855. What gave it the Sauternes name it shares with Yquem?
questions.exp: The decree of 30 September 1936 first recognised the Sauternes appellation; the list of 1855 ranked estates but left Gilette out.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026 (six searches): the decree of 30 September 1936 is the appellation's own rules at the INAO; the concrete vats, never oak, and fifteen to twenty years in vat rest on Vinfolio, the importer, Decanter and a merchant; a steel fermentation and epoxy lined vats, in one account only, are cut.

The Depression story of the 1930s is told as the family's account, from Vinfolio and the importer; the year the long ageing began, 1937 in one account, and the wartime tale of twenty seven years in vat are left out.
The family's tenure since 1710 in one account and since the nineteenth century in another is left as for generations.
Muscadelle, a few per cent, rests on two accounts; the small vats and the vats filled to the brim are cut, unconfirmed.
The label words: until 1961 the estate labelled by sweetness, Doux among them, and Crème de Tête from 1962 in one account; the label line keeps to the name of the top selection.
Gilette keeps its pick: its Crème de Tête is on the house list and the library teaches it; the family of these years is living and never named.
